statements.text: Glucagon activates hepatic glucagon receptors, stimulates glycogenolysis and raises blood glucose when adequate hepatic glycogen is present.
Raises blood glucose in severe hypoglycemia and relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle for selected diagnostic procedures when labeled.
Emergency treatment of severe hypoglycemia in pediatric and adult patients with diabetes.
Nausea and vomiting are the most common adverse reactions.
Severe hypertension can occur in pheochromocytoma; insulinoma can cause an initial glucose rise followed by exaggerated insulin release and recurrent hypoglycemia.
Anaphylactic shock and necrolytic migratory erythema during continuous infusion are rare clinically important reactions.
Adverse effects involve gastrointestinal symptoms, cardiovascular blood-pressure/heart-rate changes, hypersensitivity, glucose regulation and skin with prolonged infusion.
Contraindicated in pheochromocytoma, insulinoma and hypersensitivity to glucagon or product components.
Turn an unconscious patient on the side because vomiting can occur; give oral carbohydrate after recovery to restore glycogen and prevent recurrence.
After intramuscular administration for hypoglycemia, glucose response generally begins within minutes.
For gastrointestinal diagnostic use, effect duration is dose- and route-dependent, approximately 9 to 32 minutes across labeled regimens.
Mean elimination half-life ranges from approximately 8 to 18 minutes.
Glucagon is degraded in liver, kidney and plasma.
Intramuscular dosing reaches mean peak concentration at about 13 minutes and subcutaneous dosing at about 20 minutes; mean volume of distribution is 0.25 L/kg.
Beta-blockers can cause a transient increase in pulse and blood pressure after glucagon; indomethacin can blunt or reverse hyperglycemia, and warfarin effect may increase.
Check glucose response, airway safety and recurrence of hypoglycemia after treatment.
Case reports and small observational studies over decades have not identified a major-birth-defect or miscarriage signal, and small studies found no early placental transfer.
Human-milk data are unavailable, but glucagon is a peptide expected to be digested to amino acids and is unlikely to harm an exposed infant.
The product is labeled for severe hypoglycemia in pediatric patients; dose is weight-based below the specified threshold.
Clinical studies included too few adults 65 or older to establish differential response; other experience has not identified a consistent difference.
Overdose may cause nausea, vomiting, hypokalemia and increased blood pressure or pulse; provide supportive management and monitor potassium and blood pressure.
Glucagon raises glucose by hepatic glycogenolysis; it is also a recurring off-label toxicology exam answer for beta-blocker overdose, which requires separate evidence.

statements.text: Haloperidol antagonizes central dopamine receptors; blockade in motor pathways explains extrapyramidal effects.
Reduces manifestations of psychotic disorders and controls tics and vocal utterances in Tourette disorder.
Management of manifestations of psychotic disorders and control of tics/vocal utterances in Tourette disorder.
Extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism, sedation and orthostatic hypotension can occur.
Tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, QT prolongation/torsades and sudden death are serious risks.
Torsades de pointes, sudden death, neuroleptic malignant syndrome and blood dyscrasias are uncommon but severe.
Toxicity spans extrapyramidal/tardive neurologic, cardiovascular rhythm, endocrine/prolactin, hematologic and thermoregulatory systems.
Older patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have increased mortality; haloperidol is not approved for this use.
Contraindicated in severe toxic CNS depression or coma from any cause and in hypersensitivity to haloperidol.
Use the lowest effective dose and regularly reassess for tardive dyskinesia, NMS, falls and cardiac risk.
Haloperidol undergoes hepatic metabolism, including CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 pathways.
QT-prolonging drugs and electrolyte disturbances increase arrhythmia risk; CYP3A4/CYP2D6 inhibitors can raise exposure, while levodopa effects may be antagonized.
Monitor extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, temperature/rigidity, orthostatic blood pressure and ECG/electrolytes when cardiac risk is present.
Neonates exposed during the third trimester can develop extrapyramidal or withdrawal symptoms.
The selected label states that infants should not be nursed during haloperidol treatment.
Safety and effectiveness are not established in the Pediatric Use section; the dosage section contains historical guidance for ages 3 to 12 and states it is not intended below age 3.
Older adults, especially women, have the highest tardive-dyskinesia prevalence and generally require lower, more gradual dosing.
Overdose commonly causes severe extrapyramidal reactions, hypotension and sedation; provide airway/circulatory support and ECG monitoring.
High-potency typical antipsychotic: D2 blockade with prominent EPS, tardive dyskinesia, NMS and QT risk.

items.text: Heparin：Heparin類活化antithrombin → 抑制IIa與Xa；LMWH較偏Xa。
用於：DVT/PE、ACS、橋接抗凝、孕婦可用抗凝（不過胎盤）。
考點：UFH監aPTT、可用protamine；HIT是大考點。

statements.text: Heparin binds antithrombin and accelerates inhibition of activated coagulation factors, particularly IIa and Xa.
Produces immediate anticoagulation after intravenous administration and prevents propagation of thrombi.

Prophylaxis and treatment of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, anticoagulation in selected cardiac/vascular procedures and prevention of clotting in blood samples or extracorporeal circuits as labeled.
Bleeding, injection-site irritation, thrombocytopenia and transient aminotransferase elevations can occur.
Major hemorrhage, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with or without thrombosis (HIT/HITT), hyperkalemia and osteoporosis with prolonged high-dose exposure are important risks.
Skin necrosis, anaphylactoid reactions and alopecia are uncommon clinically important reactions.
Major toxicity domains are bleeding, immune hematologic HIT/HITT, metabolic hyperkalemia and bone loss with prolonged high-dose exposure.
Contraindicated in uncontrolled active bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia or a history of HIT/HITT, and when appropriate coagulation monitoring cannot be performed for full-dose therapy.
Confirm product strength to avoid fatal medication errors and promptly stop heparin if HIT/HITT is suspected.
Anticoagulant action is immediate after intravenous administration and delayed after subcutaneous administration.
The plasma half-life is dose-dependent and generally about 0.5 to 2 hours.
Unfractionated heparin does not undergo enzymatic degradation.
Clearance is biphasic, with rapid saturable binding/uptake and slower first-order elimination mainly through liver and reticuloendothelial cells.
Heparin is not orally absorbed, is highly bound to antithrombin and other plasma proteins, and has a volume of distribution of about 0.07 L/kg.
Antiplatelet agents, NSAIDs and other anticoagulants increase bleeding; IV nitroglycerin can reduce apparent heparin effect.
For therapeutic unfractionated heparin monitor aPTT or anti-Xa according to protocol, platelet count, hematocrit/hemoglobin, bleeding and potassium in at-risk prolonged therapy.
Heparin does not cross the placenta, but use preservative-free formulations in pregnancy when indicated.
Use preservative-free product in neonates and infants because benzyl alcohol can cause serious toxicity.
Adults over 60 may have higher heparin levels, longer aPTT and more bleeding and may require lower doses.
Protamine sulfate neutralizes heparin after clinically significant overdose; dose according to the recent heparin exposure and monitor for protamine reactions.
UFH potentiates antithrombin against IIa and Xa, is monitored with aPTT/anti-Xa and is reversed with protamine.
